10-year research plan, 2026 to 2035

Cybersecurity in Organizations: Employees' Protective and Risky Security Behaviors

Noah 10-Year Plan: A Research Program in Behavioral Information Security

Huan (Noah) Nguyen
PhD Student, Business Information Technology, Pamplin College of Business, Virginia Tech

The plan in one question

Why do employees turn workplace security rules into protection, or into risk?

Employees often bend or go around security controls to get their work done, especially when the work is urgent or the approved system fails. My 10-year plan studies these choices: what drives them, how to improve them, and what they lead to.

The program at a glance

Following Venkatesh (2021), these diagrams show the program step by step, from its overall structure to the mechanisms behind each research question. They are conceptual maps of the program, not research models.

Research Program: Topic Area, Overarching Question, Stream, and Research Questions

Research Interests: Research Questions and Research Topics

The overview adapts Venkatesh's overview of technology adoption. Employees react to a security control, form an intention to act protectively or riskily, and then act. The behavior feeds back into later reactions, for example when a workaround becomes a habit.

Overview of My Research Program

My dissertation sits at the core of the program. Employees react to a security control, such as a ban, a usage limit, a mandate to use AI, or a system outage, and choose a protective or risky behavior (RQ1).

Dissertation Research

Contingencies come next (RQ1). The same control can lead to different behaviors depending on how urgent the work is, whether systems are disrupted, the employee's role and status, whether use is mandated, how visible the behavior is, what peers do, and national culture (Vance et al., 2020).

Contingencies

Interventions aim to enhance protective behavior and reduce risky behavior (RQ2). These include bans and sanction messages, but also accountability cues, approved alternatives, and request routes that give employees a protective way to get their work done.

Interventions

Consequences and broader issues complete the program (RQ3). These include task and care continuity, data exposure, and breaches, as well as information assurance and resilience and the role of security leaders such as CISOs and CIOs.

Consequences and Broader Issues

The gaps point to the mechanisms that each research question must explain. Each research question branches into the mechanisms the plan will study, with the main theory lens and gap number in italics.

Research Questions and Mechanisms

The problem

48%of employees use AI tools that their employer has not approved (Rosquin, 2026)
73.8%of ChatGPT use at work runs on personal accounts (Cyberhaven Labs, 2024)
1 in 5organizations reported a breach due to shadow AI (IBM, 2025)
2 of 121hospital staff locked their screens as the policy required (Sarkar et al., 2020)

Organizations write security rules, approve some tools, and ban others, yet employees often go around them. In a 2026 survey of 2,001 employees in the United Kingdom and the United States, 48% said they use AI tools that their employer has not approved, and 29% said they would keep using AI even if it were banned (Rosquin, 2026). Senior staff lead this behavior. Of decision-makers, 65% use unapproved AI, against 31% of other employees.

Much of this use is out of sight of security teams. Log data from about three million workers show that personal accounts carried 73.8% of ChatGPT use at work (Cyberhaven Labs, 2024). One in five organizations reported a breach due to shadow AI, and organizations with high levels of shadow AI saw about $670,000 higher breach costs (IBM, 2025).

The same pattern appears in hospitals. In one field study, only 2 of 121 staff locked their screens as the policy required, because they would not let logins slow patient care (Sarkar et al., 2020). The pressure grows when systems fail. In each case, what a security control achieves depends on what employees choose, and each choice has a protective side and a risky side.

The gap

Prior research identifies many protective and risky behaviors. Less is known about how employees choose among them.

The field explains some drivers well, such as personal norms (Cram et al., 2019), habit (Vance et al., 2012), and peer behavior (Haag et al., 2019). It also shows six gaps, grouped by the three research questions. Under each gap is the evidence from prior work.

Drivers (RQ1)

  1. Prior work explains little about which option an employee chooses when a control blocks the work.Protection is a set of many separate behaviors (Posey et al., 2013). In an emergency department, most staff minimized their screens instead of locking them, a middle option called pseudocompliance (Sarkar et al., 2020). When a threat confuses employees, some cope in a protective way and others avoid the problem (Lins et al., 2026). Tight group norms raised conforming use and lowered workarounds, but this study was on enterprise systems, not on security controls (Wei et al., 2026). Coping theory allows several responses to the same stressor (D'Arcy et al., 2014). The theory of workarounds describes how people weigh a workaround when an obstacle blocks a goal (Alter, 2014), but it has rarely been tested with security controls as the obstacle.
  2. Theories treat a violation as self-interest, but many violations serve the work.Physicians barely responded to sanctions because the patient could not wait (Sarkar et al., 2020). Many rule breakers aim to do the job well (Morrison, 2006). Helping the work goal was the strongest reason peers excused a violation (Haag et al., 2025), and deadlines and bonuses led software staff to skip quality practices (Moody et al., 2026). Only one study measured whether deviant use achieved the task (Haag et al., 2022).
  3. Theories assume that rules apply equally to everyone, but powerful actors are controlled less.High-privilege abusers were disciplined least (Straub & Nance, 1990). Managers show more reactive computer abuse and more technological entitlement (Amo et al., 2022; Lowry et al., 2015). Peers excuse violations by high-status colleagues (Haag et al., 2025), and senior staff lead the use of unapproved AI (Rosquin, 2026).

Interventions (RQ2)

  1. Controls often move risky behavior out of sight instead of removing it.Deterrence can lead to displacement or to hiding instead of stopping (Willison et al., 2018). Enforcement moved cybercrime to countries that did not enforce (Hui et al., 2017), but displacement has rarely been tested for employees. Interface cues that made users feel identifiable reduced their intentions to violate access policies, but the study did not follow whether the behavior moved elsewhere (Vance et al., 2015). Bans on public AI tools appear to move use to personal devices (Silic et al., 2025). People who use AI at work expect to be seen as lazier and less competent, which is a barrier to disclosing the use (Reif et al., 2025).
  2. Protective effects fade within weeks or months, while risky adaptations persist.Warning adherence fell from 87% to 64% within three weeks (Vance et al., 2018). Habituation also carries over from everyday notifications to security warnings that people have never seen (Vance et al., 2025). Monitoring effects disappeared after four months (Jiang et al., 2024), and the benefit of embedded phishing training decayed (Yin et al., 2026). Password sharing that began during a storm continued afterward (Park et al., 2015).

Consequences and broader issues (RQ3)

  1. Behavioral studies rarely measure what behavior does, and firm-level studies leave employee behavior out.Policy compliance may be the wrong outcome to study, because behavior leads to an incident only through vulnerabilities and weak controls (Cram & D'Arcy, 2026). Firm-level studies explain breaches through technology and spending without observing what staff do (Angst et al., 2017; Li et al., 2023). Recent editorials call for longitudinal designs (Sarkar et al., 2026) and for research on how behavior such as shadow IT adds to organizational complexity (Schneier & Vance, 2025).

Workplace AI tools and AI agents are the new setting in which this plan studies the six gaps. Employees now share work data with AI tools, and AI agents now check, block, and approve work, so the same questions about choice, status, hidden behavior, and outcomes return in a new form.

These gaps matter in practice. When controls push behavior out of sight, organizations lose the ability to govern it. When protection fades while risky habits persist, repeated training and warnings waste time and money. When studies cannot link behavior to breaches, firms cannot tell which behaviors to target. The cost of a breach also reaches the people in the data. After a breach of state tax records, mortgage denials rose for residents of that state (Pang & Vance, 2025).

Three research questions

The overarching question is: What are the drivers and consequences of employees' protective and risky security behaviors? Three research questions follow from it.

RQ1 · Drivers

What drives employees' protective and risky security behaviors?

Objective. Explain which factors and conditions lead employees to protective or risky security behaviors.

  • Behaviors: comply, ask, report, or violate, pseudo-comply, work around, hide
  • Contexts: the technology (AI tools and other IT at work), the controls faced (bans, usage limits, mandates), and the situation (outages and disasters)
  • Mechanisms: a blocked route, work goals, justifications, status, leaders, legitimacy

Papers 1, 2, 5, 9

RQ2 · Interventions

How can employees' protective security behaviors be enhanced and risky ones reduced?

Objective. Design and test ways to enhance protective behavior and reduce risky behavior without pushing it out of sight.

  • Controls: bans and sanctions, monitoring and accountability
  • Alternatives: approved tools, request and exception routes
  • Over time: training and warnings, decay and habits

Papers 2, 6, 7, 8

RQ3 · Consequences and broader issues

What are the consequences of employees' protective and risky security behaviors, and what broader issues follow for information assurance, resilience, and security leadership?

Objective. Explain the outcomes of these behaviors for work and information, and the broader issues that follow for information assurance, resilience, and security leadership.

  • Outcomes: breaches, data exposure, task and care continuity, performance
  • Information assurance: resilience, downtime and recovery
  • Security leadership: CISO and CIO, board oversight, senior exemptions

Papers 3, 4, 5, 10

Paper 2 serves RQ1 and RQ2, and paper 5 serves RQ1 and RQ3. Six groups of conditions can change the answers to all three questions: person, situation, organization, technology, relationship, and culture.

The idea in one picture

Employees react to a security control, such as a ban, a usage limit, a mandate to use AI, or a system outage, and choose a protective or risky behavior.

Protective. Comply, ask for access or an exception, report.

Risky. Violate, pseudo-comply, work around, use shadow IT and AI, hide.

The same control can lead to different behaviors depending on how urgent the work is, whether systems are disrupted, the employee's role and status, whether use is mandated, how visible the behavior is, what peers do, and national culture (Vance et al., 2020).

Both paths lead to consequences for the work, the data, and the firm. The three tags in the picture show where each research question sits.

Methods

The plan uses multi-wave surveys, vignette and field experiments, interviews, and field and log data, such as incident and downtime records and donated chat-log counts. Interviews establish each phenomenon before experiments test it. Data come from the United States and Vietnam, where sanctions and excuses may work differently (Vance et al., 2020).

Expected contributions

Theory

From IT security behavior to AI and agentic security behavior

The plan extends research on security behavior to AI tools and AI agents. It uses the term agentic security behavior for how employees and AI agents act together under security rules. In this setting, the plan explains which option employees choose when a control blocks the work (gap 1). It treats many violations as attempts to get the work done, not only as self-interest (gap 2). It also shows how status and leaders change which rules apply to whom (gap 3).

Method

From survey intentions to real behaviors and incident records

The plan links observed employee behavior to incident, downtime, and breach records (gap 6). It pairs surveys with donated chat-log data and repeated waves with the same people. It measures specific actions rather than one compliance score.

Practice

From controls that fade or hide risk to adaptive approaches

Security leaders will learn which controls, warnings, and AI guardrails reduce risky behavior and which only move it out of sight (gap 4). They will also learn how to adapt warnings over time so that the effect does not fade (gap 5). Hospitals will learn how to keep care running during disruption without losing control of patient data.
